draft.title: Cognitive dissonance
card: Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort we feel when two of our beliefs clash, or when our actions clash with our beliefs. Festinger described it in the 1950s.
The discomfort pushes us to reduce it. The more the clash matters to us, the stronger the push.
Change the belief
adjust the belief so it fits the action, such as deciding that the action is not really harmful.
Change the action or explain it away
stop the action so it fits the belief, or add a reason that excuses the gap, such as "everyone does it".
draft.remember: Dissonance is the discomfort of a clash. People ease it by changing a belief, changing the action or excusing the gap.

a.q: Dan believes in saving money but spends his savings on a holiday. He feels uneasy. What is this feeling?
opts: Cognitive dissonance
A stereotype
A fundamental attribution error
An anchoring effect
a.why: Dan's action clashes with his belief, and the clash causes discomfort. That is cognitive dissonance. A stereotype is a belief about a group, so it does not describe a personal clash between belief and action.
a.clue: Look for a clash between what he believes and what he did.

b.q: Priya believes smoking harms health, but she smokes. She tells herself, "My grandfather smoked and lived to 90." How is she reducing dissonance?
opts: Explaining the gap away with an excuse
Changing her action by quitting smoking
Changing her belief that smoking is harmful
Removing the discomfort by ignoring the clash
b.why: Priya keeps both her belief and her action. She adds a reason that excuses the gap. She has not quit, so her action is unchanged, and she has not dropped the belief that smoking harms health.
b.clue: Check whether her belief or her action has actually changed.

b.best: Explaining the gap away with an excuse

problems.detail: The remember line splits the ways of reducing dissonance into three neat strategies. The card groups 'change the action' and 'explain it away' into a single bullet, so it only offers two headings.

The card's 'change the belief' example is 'deciding that the action is not really harmful'. The grandfather excuse could reasonably be read as Priya deciding smoking is not really harmful for her, which blurs the line between 'Changing her belief that smoking is harmful' and 'Explaining the gap away'. The card should separate the two strategies more clearly, or the stem should make plain that her belief is unchanged.

check.summary: Both answers check out, but the card lumps 'change the action' and 'explain it away' into one bullet while the remember line splits them three ways. The card's 'change the belief' example (deciding the action is not really harmful) overlaps with Priya's excuse in question b, which makes that question arguable.

proposal.title: Cognitive dissonance
card: Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort we feel when our actions clash with our beliefs. The discomfort pushes us to reduce it, and the more the clash matters to us, the stronger the push.
Change the belief
drop or soften the belief so it fits the action, such as a smoker deciding that smoking is not really harmful after all.
Change the action
stop or alter the action so it fits the belief, such as a smoker quitting.
Explain it away
keep both the belief and the action, but add a reason that excuses the gap, such as "everyone does it".
proposal.remember: A clash between belief and action feels uncomfortable, so people change one of them or excuse the gap.

a.q: Dan believes in saving money but spends his savings on a holiday. He feels uneasy. What is this feeling?
opts: Cognitive dissonance
A stereotype
A fundamental attribution error
An anchoring effect
a.why: Dan's action clashes with his belief, and the clash causes discomfort. That is cognitive dissonance. A stereotype is a belief about a group, so it does not describe a personal clash between belief and action.
a.clue: Look for a clash between what he believes and what he did.

b.q: Priya still believes smoking harms health, and she keeps smoking. She tells herself, "I'm stressed, so I need it right now." How is she reducing dissonance?
opts: Explaining the gap away with an excuse
Changing her action by quitting smoking
Changing her belief that smoking is harmful
Showing no dissonance, as her belief and action agree
b.why: Priya keeps both her belief and her action, and adds a reason that excuses the gap. Her belief has not changed, since she still thinks smoking harms health, and she has not quit. Her belief and action do clash, so there is dissonance to reduce.
b.clue: Check whether her belief or her action has actually changed.
